paras: The attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois, took place on November 9, 1881, when a mob at Adrian, in Hancock County, tried to seize a young Black farm hand from the officers bringing him back from Peoria and shot him three times. He had been accused of assaulting a farmer's wife, Mrs. Kenkel (also spelled Kunkel), and officers carried him under guard to the county jail at Carthage, where he was reported to be dying. Short wire accounts of the shooting ran in papers from Wisconsin to Mississippi and New Mexico over the next ten days.

On November 7 a Keokuk, Iowa, dispatch to the Chicago Tribune reported an "attempted outrage" near Ferris on a farmer's wife named Kenkel, committed by "a tramp" while she was alone at home. According to that report, the man threw a blanket over her head and tried to force her to the floor, but she resisted and bit him, and he fled into a cornfield. The dispatch added that he was being pursued and "if caught will be roughly dealt with."

A second Keokuk dispatch, dated November 9, identified the man as "a young negro who had been employed on a farm in the neighborhood." It said he had been arrested at Peoria that day and had confessed, and that officers then took him to Adrian, which it called "the scene of his crime." There, according to the Tribune, a mob took the prisoner from the officers and shot him three times. The officers rallied a force of men, retook him, and carried him to Carthage in a heavily guarded box-car, and no one was allowed to see him.

A differently worded brief said that after his confession he had been ordered to the jail at Carthage when the woman's neighbors tried to take him from the officers and lynch him. In this version the neighbors failed to get him and instead fired several shots, inflicting what the brief called fatal wounds, after which "a large posse" put him in a box-car and took him to jail.

The last reports placed the prisoner in the county jail at Carthage "in a dying condition." The Tribune described "intense excitement" in Adrian and in the towns the officers passed through on the way. No report of his death, of an inquest, or of arrests among the mob appears in the coverage, and none of the articles gives his name.

The Chicago Tribune printed the Keokuk dispatch on November 10 under the head "A Hard Road for a Negro Criminal to Travel," while its criminal-news deck announced "A Young Negro Desperado Fataly Shot by a Mob at Adrian, Ill." The Las Vegas Daily Gazette ran the same text on November 13 under "Fiend Finished," with "assaulted and ravished" where the Tribune had "assaulted," and decked it "A Negro Rape Fiend Riddled With Bullets in Illinois." The Gazette's next deck, naming "Wm. Russell, Negro," belonged to a separate Frankfort, Kentucky, story on the same page, not to the Adrian prisoner.

The Dallas Daily Herald carried both the November 7 item and a one-line notice that "a young negro" had ravished Mrs. Kenkel and confessed. Between November 16 and 19 a two-sentence news-in-brief paragraph, ending "His crime was a criminal assault upon a married woman," appeared in the Batesville Guard, the Richmond Democrat, the Iola Register, the Grenada Sentinel and the St. Landry Democrat. A separate "Crime" column item, spelling the name Kunkel and calling the prisoner "the bleeding brute," ran in Wisconsin and Dakota weeklies such as the River Falls Journal and the Canton Advocate. None of these reports criticized the mob, and each treated the accusation and the reported confession as fact.

The accounts differed on the alleged crime: the first Keokuk report described an attempt that Mrs. Kenkel fought off, while later versions said she was "assaulted," "ravished" or the victim of "a criminal assault." The first report, written before any arrest, also blamed "a tramp" and placed the attack near Ferris, while the later dispatches placed it at or near Adrian.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois
bases: A mob at Adrian seized or tried to seize a prisoner from officers in order to lynch him and shot him three times; he was last reported dying in jail, so this is an attempted lynching (A3, A8, A9).

Three differently worded wire versions (the Tribune's Keokuk special, the 'A mob at Adrian' brief, and the 'Kunkel' crime brief) agree that a crowd at Adrian shot a Black prisoner held by officers, though they may share a single original source (A3, A8, A9).

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran the dispatch under 'A Hard Road for a Negro Criminal to Travel' and a deck calling him 'A Young Negro Desperado', calling him 'the fiend' without criticizing the mob.
The Las Vegas Daily Gazette headed the dispatch 'Fiend Finished' and decked it 'A Negro Rape Fiend Riddled With Bullets in Illinois.'
Weekly 'Crime' columns called him 'the bleeding brute' and the complainant 'the unfortunate woman'.
Southern and western news-in-brief columns ran a flat two-sentence paragraph ending 'His crime was a criminal assault upon a married woman.'
